name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,780

entries.clue: Monsters mostly guzzle on bison’s heart (7)

indicators.note: most of the word, so GORGE loses its last letter
the heart of a word is its central letter

blocks.note: GORGE = guzzle, minus its final E

annotation.surface: Beasts gorging themselves on the innards of a bison.
annotation.walkthrough: Monsters guzzling a bison makes a coherent scene, so the wordplay hides in plain sight; the Gorgons were Medusa and her snake-haired sisters.
annotation.definitionFit: The Gorgons are the three monstrous sisters of Greek myth.

entries.clue: Bollinger manufactures bottles of Mosel? (6)

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer inside it, as a bottle holds wine

blocks.note: bolLINGER MANufactures: the answer sits across the two words

annotation.surface: A champagne house turning its hand to bottling Mosel wine.
annotation.walkthrough: Bollinger is a champagne house, so 'bottles' reads as the wine trade; the question mark marks Mosel as an example of something German.
annotation.definitionFit: The Mosel is a German river and wine region, so a Mosel wine is German.

entries.clue: I say, are you writing up boring event with touchdown zone? (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' means read the next piece from bottom to top

blocks.note: 'are you' as texters write it: R U

annotation.surface: Someone asks if you are writing up a dull match report.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Writing up' looks like one phrase about reports, but 'writing' ends the texting piece and 'up' turns YAWN over.
annotation.definitionFit: Aircraft touch down on a runway.

entries.clue: Take too many clothes off and ruin film (10)

blocks.note: to expose too much of oneself
to let too much light onto photographic film

annotation.surface: An actor strips too far and spoils the movie.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'film' as a movie; the second sense is photographic film spoiled by too much light.
annotation.definitionFit: To overexpose is to reveal too much, of a body or of a negative.

entries.clue: Quietly one pockets 2/3 of bus fare in Japan (5)

indicators.note: the outer letters take the inner piece into them
keep two of the word's three letters

annotation.surface: A passenger quietly pocketing part of the bus fare.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fare' sits beside 'bus' and looks like a ticket price, but it means food.
annotation.definitionFit: Sushi is the classic Japanese dish of vinegared rice.

entries.clue: Enthusiastic display of half-time pies and Bovril? (7)

blocks.note: the food and drink of football supporters at the interval, split 3+4

annotation.surface: Football supporters cheering over their half-time snacks.
annotation.walkthrough: Bovril is a beef-extract drink sold hot at British football grounds; the question mark flags the split into FAN FARE.
annotation.definitionFit: A fanfare is a showy flourish or display of enthusiasm.

entries.clue: Ranch dressing one genuine reason to leave restaurant in a hurry (4,5)

definitions.text: reason to leave restaurant in a hurry

indicators.note: the outer word clothes the inner pieces

annotation.surface: A diner fleeing after a genuine problem with the ranch dressing.
annotation.walkthrough: Ranch dressing is a salad dressing, which fits the restaurant, but the phrase splits: 'Ranch' is one piece and 'dressing' is an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A fire alarm is the one good reason to bolt from a restaurant mid-meal.

entries.clue: Flower with blue and white roots (4)

definitions.text: Flower with blue and white roots

blocks.note: not a bloom but something that flows: a river
not plant roots but the river's two source branches, named for these colours

annotation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom with coloured roots; it is something that flows, a river whose sources are the Blue and White Nile.
annotation.definitionFit: The Nile is formed where the Blue Nile and White Nile meet at Khartoum.

entries.clue: Wimbledon champion taking time to become US Grand Slammer? (8)

indicators.note: the champion's name takes the letter into itself

annotation.surface: A tennis champion taking time out to win another major title in America.
annotation.walkthrough: A grand slam is a tennis major, so 'Grand Slammer' seems to be a champion; slammer is slang for prison, and Alcatraz is the famous one in San Francisco Bay.
annotation.definitionFit: Alcatraz was America's most famous prison, a grand slammer indeed.

entries.clue: Close screens, partners are entangled! (8)

indicators.note: the outer word hides the inner letters behind it

blocks.note: South and North, partners at bridge

annotation.surface: Hidden behind screens, a couple are caught in a tangle.
annotation.walkthrough: In bridge, North–South and East–West are the two partnerships, so partners can be written NS or SN. 'Entangled' reads as a comment on the couple but is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something caught in a snare is tangled up in it.

entries.clue: Peeled fruit to bring to bear (5)

indicators.note: the skin comes off, here the fruit's first letter

annotation.surface: An instruction for readying fruit to eat.
annotation.walkthrough: Peeling usually strips both ends of a word; here only the O goes.
annotation.definitionFit: A gunnery sense: aiming artillery at a target by setting its distance is both ranging and bringing it to bear.

entries.clue: Poland blocks cruises at sea displaying religious clothing (9)

indicators.note: Poland's letters sit in the middle, blocking the rest
confused, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A Polish blockade of cruise ships, with clergy on deck.
annotation.walkthrough: Poland is abbreviated by its two-letter international code, and the surface's blockade of ships is really letters sitting inside other letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Surplices are the loose white vestments worn by clergy and choristers.

entries.clue: Acclaimed new nursing area of university (10)

indicators.note: a new version of the word, so its letters are rearranged
holds the extra letter inside, as a nurse holds a baby

annotation.surface: A celebrated new nursing department at a university.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a university department of nursing, but 'of university' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Academical means relating to a university or college, as in academical dress.

entries.clue: Occasionally falling from Estonia's volcano (4)

indicators.note: only now and then, so every other letter
the letters drop out of the next word

blocks.note: E s T o N i A: the odd letters

annotation.surface: Something falling now and then from a volcano in Estonia.
annotation.walkthrough: Estonia has no volcanoes; Etna is in Sicily.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Sicily's Mount Etna is one volcano among many, and Europe's most active.

entries.clue: Crestfallen or tickled about discovering oil? (10)

indicators.note: turned about, so read backwards
uncovering what lies inside the words

annotation.surface: Someone is gloomy or delighted at striking oil.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags citronella as one oil of many.
annotation.definitionFit: Citronella is an aromatic oil from lemongrass, used to repel insects.

entries.clue: Provide waffle right before I carve up pâté sandwiches (11)

indicators.note: R comes ahead of the rest
stirred up, so the letters are rearranged
the outer word holds the filling

blocks.note: the bread of the sandwich, split P…ATE

annotation.surface: A cook carves up a pâté sandwich while talking nonsense.
annotation.walkthrough: The accent on pâté is dropped to give PATE, which splits after its P to take in R and the rearranged I CARVE.
annotation.definitionFit: To prevaricate is to talk evasively, waffling to avoid the point.

entries.clue: Christian perhaps rising to speak in a flowery manner (9)

definitions.note: ELABORATE is an adjective; the definition is adverbial, describing a manner

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means read backwards

blocks.note: Christian Bale, the actor; 'perhaps' because he is one Bale of many

annotation.surface: A Christian rising in church to preach in florid language.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Christian' looks like a believer; it is a first name, pointing to the actor Christian Bale.
annotation.definitionFit: Elaborate style is ornate and detailed, like flowery speech.

entries.clue: Desk jockeys were inside and treated like pieces of meat (8)

indicators.note: jockeying moves things about, so the letters are rearranged
the next word goes into the rearranged one

annotation.surface: Office workers stuck indoors, treated like cattle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Desk jockeys' is one phrase for office workers, but 'jockeys' is working alone on DESK.
annotation.definitionFit: Skewered meat is pierced through on a spit or kebab stick.

entries.clue: Party animal turns up volume of opera lyrics (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue, the word turns over and reads bottom to top

annotation.surface: A party animal cranking up the volume on some opera.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party animal' and 'turns up volume' are both stock phrases, and each breaks apart.
annotation.definitionFit: A libretto is the book of words of an opera; the word means 'little book'.

entries.clue: Model Sierra, almost market leader in UK soon? (4,7)

indicators.note: a model is a new form, so the letters are remade
almost the whole word, so Sierra stops one letter short of its end

annotation.surface: An advert for a Ford Sierra, a car model once close to market leader.
annotation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer led the Labour Party in opposition and became UK Prime Minister in 2024, hence 'soon?' when this was set.
annotation.definitionFit: Keir Starmer was then the Labour leader expected to become Prime Minister.

entries.clue: What Detective Chief Superintendent typically did to get rank (6)

definitions.text: What Detective Chief Superintendent typically did

blocks.clueFragment: What Detective Chief Superintendent typically did
blocks.note: a senior detective typically headed, i.e. ran, the CID, the Criminal Investigation Department; split the answer 3+3

annotation.surface: A question about a senior detective's route to promotion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rank' reads as police rank, but it means stinking. The CID is the detective branch of a British police force.
annotation.definitionFit: Rancid and rank both describe food that smells off.

entries.clue: This could be Eccles High Street (6)

indicators.note: high as in drunk, so the letters reel about

annotation.surface: A town's main street, perhaps in Eccles near Manchester.
annotation.walkthrough: Eccles looks like the town near Manchester, famous for its cakes, but here it is Eccles the crossword setter.
annotation.definitionFit: Eccles is a pseudonymous crossword setter, so Eccles is an example of a setter.

entries.clue: Division is Guardian's responsibility (4)

blocks.note: an electoral district of a city, or a section of a hospital
a child in a guardian's care

annotation.surface: A newspaper's editorial desk owning up to a split.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital G makes 'Guardian' look like the newspaper; it is simply a legal guardian.
annotation.definitionFit: A ward is both an administrative division and someone under a guardian's protection.

entries.clue: Madame in on criminal network identification (6,4)

indicators.note: crooked, so the letters are twisted

annotation.surface: A madame involved in a crime ring gets identified.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Criminal network' reads as one phrase about gangs, but 'criminal' works on the words before it and 'network identification' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A domain name is the address that identifies a site on the internet.

entries.clue: Top performers regularly at the farm (1-4)

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter

blocks.note: A t T h E f A r M

annotation.surface: The best workers turn up every day at the farm.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' reads as a comment on attendance.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the first-choice side of any group is called its A-team, as opposed to the B-team.

entries.clue: Herald is bent on being heard (4)

indicators.note: the answer is what you hear, not what you read

annotation.surface: A town crier stoops as he is heard announcing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Herald' looks like a noun but is the verb: to bode is to herald, as in 'this bodes ill'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: signs that bode trouble announce it in advance, as a herald announces an arrival.

entries.clue: Basis to restrict beer and ... (9)

annotation.surface: Grounds for limiting beer and, as 26 across goes on, sex.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs the surface into 26 across; 'and' only carries it over.
annotation.definitionFit: A rationale is the basis or reasoning behind something.

entries.clue: ... sex after heading to Long Island clubs is within the law (5)

indicators.note: 'after' is about order: the word it follows comes first, so IT is placed behind the other letters
the head, or first letter, of the next word

annotation.surface: Visiting Long Island nightclubs for sex turns out to be perfectly legal.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins 25 across, but this clue stands alone. Long Island looks like one place but gives L and I separately.
annotation.definitionFit: Licit means lawful, the opposite of illicit.

entries.clue: Do ice dancing near South East London? (7)

indicators.note: dancers move round and change places, so the letters of DO ICE do too

blocks.note: SE = South East, placed next to it

annotation.surface: An invitation to go ice dancing near south-east London.
annotation.walkthrough: 'South East London' reads as a district; London is the definition, a diocese of the Church of England, flagged by the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: London is a Church of England diocese, the area under the Bishop of London.

entries.clue: The trouble and I take a circuitous route (7)

blocks.note: the trouble and strife = the wife, i.e. her, said 'er

annotation.surface: A husband and wife taking the long way round.
annotation.walkthrough: Trouble and strife is Cockney rhyming slang for wife; 'me and 'er' is how a Cockney says 'me and her', and the order swaps from the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: To meander is to wander along a winding course.
